We are meeting at a time when the world is becoming increasingly polarized and divided. The treaty bodies are operating in a rapidly changing global and political landscape, one quite different from that when the first treaty body was established over 60 years ago. In the global context, we are facing a climate in which some seek to undermine respect for international law and to promote a retreat from international committees, including in the field of human rights. Against this backdrop, we must continue to promote the importance of the human rights ecosystem and the work of the treaty body system. In a interconnected world, multilateral cooperation and universal human rights monitoring mechanisms are more important than ever. As Treaty Body members, you have all experienced the challenges that are undermining the accessibility, impact and relevance of the system. Sessions have been cut, making planning unpredictable and further complicated by late confirmations of sessions. It is in this context that, on 11 June 2026, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights launched the Global Alliance for Human Rights, a platform designed to strengthen collective action and reconnect human rights with everyday life, public decision-making and the future of our societies. The Global Alliance integrates gender equality as a core pillar across its strategic pathways. Gender equality is specifically embedded within the Human Rights in Action pathway, which seeks to tackle discrimination, eliminate gender-based violence, and elevate the voice of survivors. Initiatives under the Global Alliance apply an explicit age, gender, and diversity lens to counter global pushbacks against women's rights and girls' rights. The framework aims to hold governments accountable for implementation failure regarding gender-based violence and systematic discrimination. Madam Chair, distinguished members, As treaty bodies operate in this challenging global and political landscape, we must continue to emphasize the importance of the human rights ecosystem and the work of the treaty body system. In an interconnected world, multilateral cooperation and universal human rights monitoring mechanisms are more important than ever. As Treaty Body members, you have experienced challenges to the ecosystem accessibility, impact and relevance, cut sessions and late confirmation of sessions and visits, making planning unpredictable. While we are addressing immediate challenges arising from the financial situation, We also need to discuss possible avenues to update and strengthen the treaty body system in the long term. With this in mind, OSCHR has shared a working paper to engage all stakeholders in reform ideas so that together we can co-create the necessary solutions. That paper focuses on three key elements. One is convening the decentralized and cluster dialogues based on the eight-year cycle, number two is a simplifying state party reporting through an integrated and multilingual online report submission platform. And third is strengthening the election of treaty body members through an online application platform to increase transparency and to ensure that experts selected fulfill the highest criteria of experience and competence and independence and impartiality in line with the Addis Ababa guidelines. At the recent meeting of the chairs of the treaty bodies, the chairs concluded that the proposal needed to be discussed by the committees to identify what can be taken forward, what requires further work, and the areas where further information is required. I invite you to consider the practical elements of these proposals, including feasibility and their impact on the right holders, and to put forward your suggestions and constructive comments on the decentralized and cluster dialogues, drawing on your experience in particular with your Fiji technical cooperation session in 2025. For this or any other concrete proposal to work, we need strong commitment from the member states to ensure resources that are adequate, predictable, and match the massive task you have in helping to uphold the normative pillars of the global human rights protection architecture. Madam Chair, distinguished members, moving now to the work of the Human Rights Council, the Council's annual discussion on the integration of a gender perspective throughout the work of the Human Rights Council and that of its mechanism took place on the 29th September 2026 during its 63rd session. It focused on the theme from gender stereotypes to structural discrimination, strengthening the Human Rights Council's response. The two hour panel discussion was chaired by the President of the Human Rights Council, His Excellency Mr. Sidarto and opened by the Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, Ms. Awa Dabo, as well as by Ms. Nariadazi Gumbanzwana, Deputy Executive Director of UN Women. CEDAW, which was chaired by Roder Reddock, was one of the four panelists who made presentations. The panel discussed the effective implementation of states' legal obligation to dismantle gender stereotypes, which are embedded in and reproduced by unequal power relations in patriarchal systems. Your General Recommendation No. 41 on gender stereotypes, which you plan to adopt later in this session, will come at the right time to provide much-needed guidance to States parties implementing those obligations. Madam Chair, distinguished members, I am aware that you have a heavy programme ahead of you for the next four weeks. I therefore conclude by wishing the Committee a successful and productive session. Your expertise, independence and commitment enable the Committee to fulfil important task of ensuring that the rights enshrined in the conventions become a reality for all women and girls worldwide. I thank you for your attention and I'm going to be with you for the next four weeks so we can continue the conversation and find a way of fine-tuning and getting every day better. Thank you. Back to you, Madam Chair.
